@shahrin014 As far as I understand it, OpenCode makes use of OpenAI ChatCompletions API for servicing these requests, and does the conversion between formats (such as from OpenAI to Anthropic) behind the scenes. I don't see anything in the code that suggest this would cause any issues if a Claude model is used with Helicone. 

I think the reason they use openai-compatible as the custom provider is because it's the format that's popularly used across, so it'd have made sense to support it this way. Every other gateway/middleman provider I have used generally follows a similar approach of providing an OpenAI compatible interface, and taking care of translations behind the scenes if non-OpenAI compatible models are being invoked.

Well yes, but even so. With copilot you get everything except user input as "free". Only user input costs premium request (x multiplier).

So, if I use Opus 4.6 (x3) and ask him to do large refactoring, it will eventually hit context wall, so you then get (which will be free if using gpt5-mini) compaction + *another* 3 premium requests for continuing work and this will repeat if you have medium sized code base:

- 3 premium requests for user input
- 0 premium requests for compaction
- 3 premium requests for continuing after compaction (this is counted as user input in opencode, but it is a system/agent requests in copilot cli)
- 0 premium requests for compaction
- 3 premium requests for continuing after compaction
...and so on until agent finishes work...

While it should be:
- 3 premium requests for user input
- 0 premium requests for compaction
- 0 premium requests for continuation
- 0 premium requests for compaction
- 0 premium requests for continuation
...and so on until agent finishes work...

+1 on this. We have a concrete use case that demonstrates why native hook support matters:

### MCP secret enforcement via PreToolUse

We run [pastewatch](https://github.com/ppiankov/pastewatch) as an MCP server across 5 agents. It provides `pastewatch_read_file` / `pastewatch_write_file` tools that replace secrets with `__PW{TYPE_N}__` placeholders — secrets stay in local RAM, only placeholders hit the API.

The problem: agents default to native `Read`/`Write` and bypass redaction entirely. Advisory instructions ("please use pastewatch tools for secrets") are unreliable, especially with weaker models.

**With hooks (Claude Code + Cline today):**

A `PreToolUse` hook on `Read|Write|Edit` runs `pastewatch-cli scan --check --fail-on-severity high --file <path>`. If secrets are detected (exit 6), the hook blocks the native tool (exit 2) and tells the agent to use `pastewatch_read_file` instead. Structural enforcement — the agent has no choice.

**Without hooks (OpenCode today):**

Advisory only. The agent *might* follow the instructions in AGENTS.md, or it might use native Read and send raw API keys to the cloud. No way to enforce it.

This is a real gap. We currently recommend Cline over OpenCode for sensitive data work specifically because of hook support.

---

Regarding protocol — we use the exact same stdin/exit code protocol described in the issue. Our hooks are portable bash scripts that work in both Claude Code and Cline today. If OpenCode adopts the same protocol, they'd work without modification.
